title: Q3 Member Feedback Recap
topic: A satisfaction score collected only from people who just renewed
blurb: The product team shared this recap after the dating-app redesign.
prompt: An AI analyst wrote this launch recap. If a line reaches further than the evidence, tap it.

segments.label: The launch
segments.text: Three months ago the app launched a new matching algorithm and redesigned profile pages.

segments.label: Who we asked
segments.text: Last week we ran a satisfaction survey with 1,200 members as they completed their monthly renewal.

segments.label: The score
segments.text: 96% of those respondents rated the new experience 4 or 5 stars.

segments.label: The takeaway
segments.text: This shows the redesign has been an overwhelming success with users overall.

segments.label: Next step
segments.text: We can roll the same design out globally without further changes.

conclusion: AI recap: a 96% satisfaction score shows users overall love the redesign. Ship it globally.

flaws.original: The 96% score only describes members who just paid for another month. People who disliked the redesign were more likely to cancel and never saw the survey, so this cannot be read as a result for users overall.
flaws.corrupted: This shows the redesign has been an overwhelming success with users overall.

diagnosis_choices.label: You only surveyed people actively renewing — everyone who hated the redesign already canceled.
1,200 respondents is too small a sample to represent a global app, even if they were chosen randomly.
Three months isn't long enough for people to get used to new profiles, so the 96% score is artificially low.
Combining 4-star and 5-star ratings inflates the result; you should only count 5-star reviews.

fix_choices.label: Track overall retention/churn since launch and survey canceled users too, not just renewers.
Increase the renewal-screen survey from 1,200 members to 10,000 before rolling out globally.
Report only the share of 5-star ratings out of the 1,200 renewing members.
Wait another three months and re-survey the same 1,200 renewing members.

flaws.explanation: The people who hated the redesign were also the most likely to cancel instead of renewing. Asking only the people who stayed almost guarantees a glowing score, and it tells you almost nothing about users overall.
flaws.why_tempting: A huge sample and a 96% score look like proof. It's easy to skip past who was in the room when the question was asked.
flaws.catch_rule: Before you trust a satisfaction number, ask who never got the survey — especially anyone who already left.
flaws.hint: Look again at who was holding the phone when they were asked. Who is missing?

practice.problem: A gym texts a smiley-face survey to everyone who swipes in this month, and 94% say they love it. What's the catch?
practice.answer: People who already cancelled their membership never swipe in, so they never see the survey.

clean_segments: Three months ago the app launched a new matching algorithm and redesigned profile pages.
Last week we ran a satisfaction survey with 1,200 members as they completed their monthly renewal.
96% of those respondents rated the new experience 4 or 5 stars.
That figure describes renewing members only. It cannot be read as a result for users overall, because people who cancelled were never asked.
Before a global rollout, we should also hear from members who left or did not renew.
clean_conclusion: 96% of renewing members were happy — not 96% of users overall.

diagnosis: Launching a new matching algorithm and redesigned profiles at the same time makes it impossible to know which worked.
Three months ago is too recent — matching algorithms need a full year to produce real couples.
Launching without a 50/50 control group means you can't tell if 96% beat the old design.
Users always dislike UI redesigns at first, so three months biases ratings downward.
fix: Split the matching algorithm and the profile redesign into two separate tests.
Compare renewal-rate changes against the three months before launch.
Wait a full 12 months before grading a dating-app algorithm.
Hold back 20% of users on the old design as a baseline.

diagnosis: 1,200 members is only a tiny sliver of the app's users, so the margin of error makes 96% meaningless.
Surveying right at the renewal screen interrupts checkout and makes annoyed users rate lower.
Running the survey only for one week misses users whose billing dates fall in the other three weeks.
Asking people to rate the app right after paying biases them toward justifying their payment.
fix: Run the renewal survey across all four weeks of the billing cycle.
Move the survey out of the checkout screen into an email a week later.
Sample 1,200 users randomly from *everyone* who was active before launch, including churned accounts.
Boost the sample size to 5,000 renewals for tighter error bars.

diagnosis: 96% giving 4 or 5 stars hides the distribution — most of them might be lukewarm 4s instead of 5s.
A 5-point star scale doesn't capture whether users actually got more matches under the new algorithm.
4% of 1,200 is 48 unhappy renewers, which proves even paying users dislike the redesign.
96% is suspiciously high, which means bots must have filled out the renewal survey.
fix: Break out 5-star vs 4-star ratings separately instead of combining them.
Track actual match and reply rates instead of star ratings.
Investigate the 48 low-star renewers before claiming 96% satisfaction.
Check for duplicate survey submissions from the same accounts.

diagnosis: Rolling out globally without localizing the profile design ignores regional dating norms.
Even if 96% of renewers love it, you should roll out to 10% of global markets first as a canary.
Global rollout doesn't need further changes only if the churn rate actually dropped too.
You can't roll out globally until the other 4% of respondents are satisfied.
fix: Pause the global rollout until you compare overall churn before vs after launch.
Test the redesign in two new countries first before a full global launch.
Localize the profile prompts for each region before rolling out.
Wait for churned-user feedback to fix what drove cancelers away.
